articles.text: Each election cycle the Piedmont Post provides extensive coverage for residents to learn about each candidate for informed voting. For this year’s races, the first four weeks of our coverage will alternate between City Council and School Board weekly. This week, City Council candidates received two questions and the following week two different questions will be asked of all school board candidates. When the election heats up in October the Post will asks questions of all candidates in both races, weekly. Week 1 Questions 1. If elected, what are your plans for housing in Piedmont? What would additional housing in Piedmont cost and what would it look like? (mixed use/ single family homes/ market rate apartments, etc.) 2. What do you see as some of Piedmont’s critical infrastructure needs and what are your plans for reinvestment or repair? The six city council candidates vying for three open seats were sent these questions on Friday, September 9, and were asked to reply with 150-word responses. BETSY ANDERSON, Incumbent 1) Housing My goal is to promote transparency and help Piedmont retain local control of our housing policies. Local control includes design standards necessary to maintain Piedmont’s charm and character. To keep local control, the City must comply with state housing laws. Every eight years, Piedmont, like all California cities, is required by the State to prepare a comprehensive Housing Element document. In this cycle, the City is required to identify where 587 units of new housing, representing many different income levels, could potentially be built. The City is not required to build housing - just identify where it could be built. It’s up to individual Piedmont property owners to determine if it is in their best interest to build additional housing on their property. It is speculative at this point to predict costs. My plan is to continue communicating with residents about this process and about the importance of retaining local control. 2) Infrastructure The short answer is that ALL of Piedmont’s city facilities are old and outdated. Over its one-hundred year history, the City has adapted to donated spaces and made relatively minor renovations to city facilities. Given the lack of investment, it is not surprising that many of our facilities are cramped, inefficient, and no longer meet the needs of our dedicated city staff and community members. During my time on Council, we have made a concerted effort to address our aging facilities. We have set aside significant funding for facilities maintenance, voted to pass a bond to rebuild the defunct Piedmont Community Pool, and we are now in the process of renovating the Police and Fire Dispatch Center. I want to help Piedmont successfully complete these projects and work with city staff and community members

articles.text: On Wednesday, September 7, the League of Women Voters of Piedmont and Piedmont Connect continued their Climate Speaker Series featuring a presentation from fire reporter and founding member of Watch Duty Sarah Paul. She focused her presentation on how wildfires start and spread, how to prepare for potential wildfires, and ways to stay informed about climate hazards and threats. Watch Duty is a wildfire awareness app and nonprofit that aims to build a “free, open, and un-editorialized emergency alert system,” according to its website. Paul has spent most of her career focused on wildfire prevention and analysis, both as an Arson Task force member for communities throughout Sonoma County and as a Community Wildfire Mitigation Specialist. She initially became involved in the midst of the Tubbs Fire in 2017 when a friend in Sonoma County with little information about the encroaching fire, eventually made a perilous escape through the flames. Paul saw her friend’s ordeal as a critical opportunity to improve communication and connectivity in the face of natural disasters. To effectively overcome climate issues, it’s critical to understand how a wildfire starts, or understand its behavior, said Paul, who explained that the three main causes of fires are fuel, oxygen and heat. In light of these factors, Paul astutely identified defensible space and home hardening as keys to limiting a fire’s fuel and thus limiting its spread. Defensible space refers to exterior protection by removing or cutting back any dry vegetation around a structure that could provide fuel for a potential wildfire while home hardening refers to protection inside like strengthening the roof, structural beams, decks or fences to increase resistance to heat, embers or flames. In many instances, large wildfires will create ember storms that, when carried by summer of fall winds, can massively increase the spread and destruction of fires in rural or unincorporated areas. In the event that all these prevention methods do not withstand the natural elements, it is important to be as prepared as possible in the event of a catastrophe. As Paul identifies, it’s safe to assume that electrical power and cell service will be nonexistent and most roads will be clogged if not entirely impassable. It’s best, especially if you live in rural areas, to get to know your neighbors and have multiple escape routes in the event of rapidly spreading fire. In the event of a large wildfire, time is of the essence which makes clear, concise plans critically important. Paul refers to a company called Zone Haven which has contracts with several Bay Area counties to set up evacuation zones. Paul also points to portable batteries, N95 masks and air purifiers with HEPA filters as useful wildfire preparation items. Watch Duty can provide live updated information about fires from multiple sources. Often there are several entities reporting on a wildfire – some from a county, some from a fire department, some from the state. Watch Duty compiles all that information to give users the most complete picture about the fire and its spread. For more information about Watch Duty, go to watchduty.org. You can view Sarah Paul’s complete presentation on YouTube by searching for Wildfire Mitigation in the Bay Area: What Can Be Done? “Dude says we’ve matured from ‘Old Boys’ to ‘Old Geezers.”

Paul saw her friend’s ordeal as a critical opportunity to improve communication and connectivity in the face of natural disasters. To effectively overcome climate issues, it’s critical to understand how a wildfire starts, or understand its behavior, said Paul, who explained that the three main causes of fires are fuel, oxygen and heat. In light of these factors, Paul astutely identified defensible space and home hardening as keys to limiting a fire’s fuel and thus limiting its spread. Defensible space refers to exterior protection by removing or cutting back any dry vegetation around a structure that could provide fuel for a potential wildfire while home hardening refers to protection inside like strengthening the roof, structural beams, decks or fences to increase resistance to heat, embers or flames. In many instances, large wildfires will create ember storms that, when carried by summer of fall winds, can massively increase the spread and destruction of fires in rural or unincorporated areas. In the event that all these prevention methods do not withstand the natural elements, it is important to be as prepared as possible in the event of a catastrophe. As Paul identifies, it’s safe to assume that electrical power and cell service will be nonexistent and most roads will be clogged if not entirely impassable. It’s best, especially if you live in rural areas, to get to know your neighbors and have multiple escape routes in the event of rapidly spreading fire. In the event of a large wildfire, time is of the essence which makes clear, concise plans critically important. Paul refers to a company called Zone Haven which has contracts with several Bay Area counties to set up evacuation zones. Paul also points to portable batteries, N95 masks and air purifiers with HEPA filters as useful wildfire preparation items. Watch Duty can provide live updated information about fires from multiple sources. Often there are several entities reporting on a wildfire – some from a county, some from a fire department, some from the state. Watch Duty compiles all that information to give users the most complete picture about the fire and its spread. For more information about Watch Duty, go to watchduty.org. You can view Sarah Paul’s complete presentation on YouTube by searching for Wildfire Mitigation in the Bay Area: What Can Be Done? articles.text: In contrast to the weather-worn, unattributed aphorism, “There ain’t no such thing as a free lunch”, the California legislature approved and is now implementing a free breakfast and lunch program for all students in all grades in public schools. California is the first state to move forward with the ambitious program. To adhere to mandatory participation in the program to start the year Piedmont schools have eliminated food sales and are offering free meals only. Approximately 75% of the funding comes from the state and is augmented by a federal program. The two sources will reimburse Piedmont School District roughly $2.60 per breakfast and $4.50 per lunch. The school has set aside $250,000 in unrestricted funds to supplement the “$250,000 is what we’re earmarked. We’re hoping we won’t need to do that. At the moment that is our number, given the cost of food, I think we may need to increase our staffing,” said PUSD’s Chief Financial Officer Ruth Alahydoian. The combined number of free lunches given out at Piedmont’s three elementary schools was around 600 per day as of September 1, and the middle and high school combined for 500 free daily lunches. Approximately 350 free breakfasts were provided in the elementary schools, and an average of 300 breakfasts were given during the brunch period for middle and high school students. “There are a lot of different factors at play. Right now we’re just providing very basic offerings. I know that that’s going to get adjusted, because our goal is to get as many kids eating as possible,” said Alahydoian. Alahydoian explained that calculating the percentage of students having school lunches in the past is tricky. In previous years students would commonly buy a single drink or snack, and now they will receive a whole meal. Cafeterias in past years would break even or make a small profit, largely from single drink sales. Without that revenue, the school district faces the likely need for a $250,000 supplement. The nutrition program falls under Alahydoian’s responsibility because it is considered part of “business services.” She has been on the front lines of the program and helped serve food in the high school cafeteria to start the year. The school district has added another mid-management job to its payroll, and has hired Gitara Spinks as Director of Food Service, working under the direction of Alahydoian. Students at Beach Elementary School line up to grab their lunches under the new universal food program. Whole Wheat Pullman Bread or Roll Chicken Salad, Egg Salad, Sliced Roasted Turkey Chicken Caesar Salad w/ Caesar Dressing & Croutons At the elementary level, parents choose meals for their kids online. As of September 1, all high school meals were open with no requirement to sign up. In recent years, Piedmont School District has partnered with a vendor Choice Lunch, which delivered hot food to the elementary school if ordered in advance. To start the year Choice Lunch is not participating as a vendor in the state free lunch program, the district now uses the vendor Lunch Master. Since every public school must participate in the program, there has been an enormous demand, and vendors are scrambling to meet the need.

articles.text: Disruption has a negative connotation to it, e.g. the kid in class who keeps talking, or the dog barking outside. But industries have long lauded innovation so new and unique that it disrupts our lives and changes the way we as a society do things. Our lives as humans (children included) can use some disruption now and again too. Something to shake up our status quo and leave us with an undeniable better. When we detach from sneaky influences like cool kids, advertisements and what others view as valuable, we allow space for new identities to take root. For adults, disruption can come in many forms, from an Eat Pray Love style journey At Camp Augusta nearly all activities are based upon creativity, creating a sense of wonder. Summer camp challenges children’s preconceived ideas of themselves, allowing them to build a newer, truer identity. around the globe. to quitting social media for a week. For children, the idea of disruption is trickier; they simply do not have the same level of autonomy to make change in their lives. What children do have, however, is summer camp, which lifts children out of everything familiar and plops them down in a foreign landscape designed to both care for and challenge them. Camp disrupts the sneaky stories children tell themselves, ones often mistaken for truth because they came from parents, friends, or teachers. For example, a parent may accidentally send the message that being away from home is scary, which the child accepts as true and fears crying before bed. Then when they make it through the session without any tears, they realize they are braver and more independent than they gave themselves credit for. Take another common example. articles.text: Highlanders beat San Leandro 5-2 prior to Fresno tourney The Highlanders’ girls’ tennis team traveled to Fresno to compete in the 2022 California Tennis Classic on Friday and Saturday, September 9-10. Playing in sweltering heat, they lost to Buchanan High 5-2 and Palos Verdes 6-0 on Friday, but rallied on Saturday for a 5-1 win over Clovis East and 5-2 over Bishop O’Dowd. “We lost both on Friday but recovered with a swim in the afternoon and a good dinner at BJs Restaurant. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont struggled to deal with Berkeley’s Zada Sanger (left) in Monday’s loss. Shelby Cavenaugh (13) and Elena Stevens (11) go up for the block. Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team took a 3-1 loss against league opponent Berkeley on Monday, September 12 at home . Five days earlier they lost by the same score to Skyline in a non-conference match at the Titans’ home gym. The pair of matches brings Piedmont’s record to 5-5. “This week, we’re going to practice a whole lot more on serve and receive. We were struggling a lot in that and that’s really the bread-and-butter of the game. I don’t think we were ready for fast-paced balls like we faced here. The tempo of Berkeley is zero-tempo and we’re working on faster-tempo sets so we can match that same energy,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. 3-1 loss to Berkeley The Yellowjackets won the first set 25-13 and took the second set 25-16. Piedmont bounced back in the third set to win 25-20 but dropped the fourth 25-15. Berkeley’s attack was led by an onslaught of spikes by outside hitters Zada Sanger and Elle Walker, who accumulated 28 total kills between them. The program is also led by former Piedmont coach and assistant Athletic Director Alison West, which marked her third win in as many attempts against the Highlanders. “Berkeley has two big time hitters and we tried to change up our rotation a couple of times to be successful. First set, we weren’t prepared; second set, we moved some things; third set we were ready and in it, but fourth set we got a bit distracted with outside factors. We need to learn to control what we can control,” said Cardenas. In the first set, things started 2-2 between the two sides but Berkeley jumped to a 6-2 lead and never looked back. The Yellowjackets eventually went on an 11-2 scoring run to extend the gap to 14-6 and closed the set by taking four of the final six points, 25-13. Piedmont led 8-5 at the start of the second set and held its last advantage at 11-10. From there, BHS scored four straight to go ahead 14-11. The Highlanders narrowed the deficit to one-point at 16-15 but the Jackets went on a 7-0 scoring run to jump ahead 23-14 and finished with two of the last three points. In Piedmont’s 25-20 win in the third set, they got off to a 3-1 start thanks to a service error, a block by Shelby Cavenaugh, and an ace by Sadie Town. With the set at 7-5, PHS went on a six point run which included kills by Tara Kothari and Maddy Mullin. Berkeley eventually battled back to tie the set at 18-18, but scored the final seven of nine points with kills by Elena Stevens, Cavenaugh, and a set-winning block by Eden Lorin. In the fourth set, Piedmont led 2-1 but couldn’t retain the lead. The two sides traded points until Berkeley led 9-8, at which point they went on a 9-1 scoring run to go up 18-9. At 19-11, BHS scored six of the last 10 points. Final stats: Kothari had five kills. Cavenaugh had seven kills and two blocks. Town four kills, one block, and two aces. Stevens had two kills and two blocks. Lorin had three kills, one ace, and one block. Mullin had two kills and a block. Bree DeYoung had one kill. Bauer Peterson had one ace. 3-1 loss to Skyline Piedmont’s trailed after the first two sets, falling 25-18 and 25-18 in back to back sets. The Highlanders battled back to a 25-20 win in the third set, but lost the clinching third set win for the Titans, 25-15. articles.text: Win vs. Pinole Valley; losses to Alhambra, Berkeley Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team won one of four matches at the Newark Memorial Tournament on Friday and Saturday, September 9-10. Their sole victory came against , Pinole Valley 10-3 in the opening round on Friday, They followed with an 8-2 semifinals loss to Alhambra on Saturday and a barnburner 5-4 loss in the 3rd place game with Berkeley later in the day. The win over Pinole Valley marked PHS’ first of the year. Impressive performances came from Katarina Melian and Odessa Dando, who combined for 10-3 win over Pinole Valley The Highlanders scored the game’s opening goal when Melian sent in a shot from the hole set position with 5:28 left in the first quarter, coming six seconds after drawing an exclusion penalty. Melian scored again in close range with 3:10 left in the quarter and two minutes later landed her hat trick goal with 1:06 remaining. Odessa Dando made it 4-0 on a solo breakaway with 37 seconds on the clock. In the second quarter, Piedmont struck again shortly after forcing a turnover when Julia Montes sent an assist to Rosie Feldman to make it 5-0 with 5:16 left in the second quarter. Two minutes later, Feldman forced a turnover by stealing a sloppy pass before assisting Dando, 6-0. About 30 seconds later, Montes scored on a lob from the left wing to make it 7-0. Photos courtesy of Golden State Rowing Club Golden State Rowing Club is a new club program started by James Kwan, a Piedmont High grad in 2010. The newest entry into the sport of crew (rowing) is Golden State Rowing Club. Founded by James Kwan, Piedmont HS Class 2010, and a former Princeton rower, the club is already attracting athletes around town by providing a personal experience. “What I’ve observed is that rowing is an amazing sport that needs to get spread out to more kids. It’s also putting forth a different experience with the sport. In my experience through high school, clubs, and in college, the rowing experience isn’t personalized. At times, you can feel like a cog in a wheel. Our goal [at Golden State] is to provide a community-based experience to make them successful in the sport and beyond,” said Kwan. Kwan formerly was with Oakland Athletic Rowing Society (OARS) and helped them achieve great heights over the summer. At the Junior National Championships in June, Kwan coached a quadruple scull to a third-place finish. The same pair won the Southwest Regional Championships in May, considered the sports’ State title. His goal with Golden State Rowing Club is to provide a more inclusive and community oriented program for athletes while still providing a premier destination for top competition. “Right now, I’m off to help one of our athletes study [for] the ACT and then go work on college essays. We want to build a full program that helps young adults take their next step,” said Kwan. “Starting Golden State Rowing was to create a community-based experience that doesn’t exist widely in sports. It fills some of the gaps that we see elsewhere. It definitely pushes you hard and at the same time fits in with whatever our athletes are doing in high school, It helps develops them into a well-rounded person,” he continued. Although Kwan has helped students win medals at prestigious events, he confirms that Golden State is open to all skill levels from grades 8th through 12th. “We are open to every kind of athlete. We row all different boat classes with boats from one-person to as many as nine. However, it’s my belief that developing in one- or two-person boats help build the critical skills you need to be fast in any team boat,” said Kwan. “Another part is that we build athletes who continue to love and are excited by the sport. We think we can get students introduced to the sport and reach the next level by developing them in the one, two, and four-person boats,” said Kwan. It would be far from the first time Kwan developed rowers without any experience in the sport. One example is PHS junior Zachary Feldstein, who qualified for the Junior Nationals last spring in the single scull in his first year of rowing. “Rowing is a sport which many athletes tend to find later on in life. A lot of the competitors have, at most, three or four years of experience. By getting a lot of individualized attention, you can make a lot of progress in your rowing technique in a year or less, like we had with Zach. I’ve had many athletes throughout the last few years, who had no rowing experience at the start of the year, and end the year at the National Championships, Regional ChamJames Kwan (right) after the OARS U17 quadruple scull placed third at Junior Nationals. articles.text: The Mosquito Fire in the Tahoe and El Dorado National Forests expanded on Tuesday, September 6 outside Foresthill and as of Tuesday night is now up to 50,330 acres – over 78 square miles – with 25 percent containment. It has officially destroyed 46 structures. Smoke from the blaze blanketed the Lake Tahoe region over the weekend, causing the cancellation of a scheduled high school football game with Piedmont and North Tahoe HS in Tahoe City. “The Mosquito Fire continues to advance steadily to the east in heavily forested areas with extremely dry vegetation. Crews continue to construct indirect lines and utilize existing road systems ahead of the advancing fire to cut off the fire’s growth to the east,” wrote CalFire on its incident report. As of yesterday, September 13, fire officials stated that the fire picked up in activity due to high winds in the area. “Fire behavior Tuesday was active, consisting of uphill runs, group torching, and short-range spotting. As expected, the inversion lifted and the air cleared early, resulting in fire growth, particularly on the east and northeastern sides of the fire. Breezy southwest winds throughout the fire area increased fire activity,” according to Inciweb.org, an official government database for wildfires. Fire behavioral analyst Jonathan Pangburn describes that the recent winds pushed smoke out of the region which enabled fire to spread faster due to fresh oxygen. “Unfortunately, we’ve had a turn of events and the southwest winds is starting to move the Photo courtesy of U.S. Forest Service Winds on Tuesday, September 13 caused a large plume of smoke from the Mosquito Fire. Photo courtesy of YubaNet Fire News The Mosquito Fire has been raging for the last week and has now covered more than 50,000 acres. Photo courtesy of YubaNet Fire News The blaze is near Foresthill in Placer County. smoke out of area, which allows fresh oxygen to the area. That unfortunately is going to lead to a slight uptick in the fire behavior,” said Pangburn. The Placer County Sheriffs Department has evacuated a total of 6,258 residents with 90 declining evacuation orders. According to Cal Fire spokesman Scott McLean, yesterday’s events caused concern from officials that the blaze was quickly approaching Foresthill while some residents have refused to leave. “They have the right to stay, and the sheriff in both counties has made it very clear, (if) you leave your property in an evacuated area and the sheriff sees you, you will be escorted out or dealt with appropriately. We get it, we understand it. But the best thing to do is leave,” said McLean, in the Sacramento Bee. The fire increased containment from 18 percent to 25 by Tuesday night. Cal Fire operations section chief Landon Haack said they’ve been able to contain things south of Foresthill Road through “significant” efforts. “As of right now, the fire is still contained to the south of Foresthill Road and ridge below Todd Valley,” said Haack. “There’s a pretty significant firefight going on out there. They’re trying really hard to hold that fire in that box right there. As of right now, we don’t have any reports of fire on the north side of Foresthill Road.”

articles.text: The 22nd annual Piedmont Jazz Festival will take place in Piedmont Main Park this Sunday, September 18 from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. as part of the city’s annual Harvest Festival. A large stage will be installed in the Main Park, making viewing and listening easy for everyone. This year’s festival will feature Forte, a Latin tinged force of nature that includes strong vocals and a tight horn section. Forte played the Festival several years ago and literally “blew a fuse” in the sound system such that the show had to stop for several minutes while the sound technicians adjusted the equipment to capture Forte’s sound. Newly emerged from a pandemic hiatus, the Festival will be an opportunity for the public to hear Forte and their tight high-powered sound. Forte will be followed by the big-band sound of the Albany Jazz Band in its fifth appearance in town. The band has been performing at concerts and dances in the San Francisco Bay Area since 1996 performing a repertoire that includes instrumentals and vocals that span classic and contemporary big band music, Latin, and pop. The Albany Jazz Band performs as its original 20-piece Big Band format and in a newer 10-piece format. Since 2005, the Albany Jazz Band has been led by Bob Levenson as music director. Band members are drawn from throughout the Bay Area. The bands rehearse every week and both maintain active performance schedules. Sunday’s festival will open with the Piedmont High School Jazz Orchestra under the baton of Andria Mullan, band director at the high school and middle school, and a talented horn player. Also appearing this year will be Juvenoia, a Piedmont based rock trio composed of Jackson Lommen (bass and vocals), Alina Shahid, (guitar), and Torsten Olsen (drums). Schedule of bands 12:00 p.m. Piedmont High School Jazz Band 1:00 p.m. Forte (16-piece band): 2:00 p.m. Albany Big Band. 3:00 p.m. Juvenoia The Jazz Festival, organized by Greg Slatoff, is free and provides the opportunity to celebrate Piedmont’s musical talent amid fun, food and friends. articles.text: In his early teens, Duane Allman regularly “borrowed” his younger brother Gregg’s Sears Silvertone guitar and played it endlessly. When Duane wrecked his little Harley 165 motorcycle, he sold the remnants to get enough money to buy a Les Paul Junior guitar. He ended up primarily playing Les Paul guitars. Early bands founded by Duane and Gregg include The Misfits, The Allman Joys and Hour Glass (with Paul Hornsby). In Jacksonville, Florida in 1969, Duane and Gregg formed The Allman Brothers Band. The most notable musicians in The Allman Brothers Band were Duane Allman, Dickey Betts and Chuck Leavell. Duane played slide blues guitar, in open E tuning (E-AE-G#-B-E) and open A tuning (E-A-E-A-C#-E) and also played in standard tuning. Duane was influenced by Robert Johnson, Elmore James Junior Wells, Muddy Waters and the Miles Davis album Kind of Blue. He wouldn’t copy phrases from them verbatim, but would listen and reflect. Duane recorded with Eric Clapton, King Curtis, Aretha Franklin and others. Gregg played the Hammond organ, guitar and sang. Dickey Betts played a standard-tuned six-string guitar. He grew up listening to bluegrass, country and Western swing. Dickey’s composition In Memory of Elizabeth Reed showed harmonic and modal influences of The Allman Brothers Band jazz artists like Miles Davis and John Coltrane. Pianist Chuck Leavell joined the Allman Brothers in 1972 and played on their album Brothers and Sisters. His great rock piano solo from the song Jessica (arranged for guitar) is included in the improvised examples linked near the end of this column. Since 1985, Chuck has regularly toured and recorded with The Rolling Stones, Eric Clapton, John Mayer, George Harrison and David Gilmour. Chuck is also an expert in sustainable forestry and wrote Growing A Better America: Smart, Strong, Sustainable. Duane was killed in a motorcycle accident in 1971 at a time when the band was in the middle of recording their next album. The remaining band members named the album Eat a Peach, to summarize Duane’s answer to the question “How are you helping the revolution?” Duane replied, “I’m hitting a lick for peace, and every time I’m in Georgia I eat a peach for peace. But you can’t help the revolution, because there’s just evolution. I’m a player. And players don’t give a damn for nothing but playing….” Listen to and read my improvised examples for this column and my previous columns at: http://www.guitarimprov.com/ PostColumns.pdf The following are notes on the improvised examples. Stormy Monday improv is in The Allman Brothers style with a bit more jazz. Jessica piano solo is Chuck Leavell’s piano solo arranged for guitar. Wahoo slide solo is a friend’s original song with my Duane Allman style slide guitar. Jim Gleason is an author and guitar instructor. articles.text: The Asian Art Museum in San Francisco is currently exhibiting Filipino artist Carlos Villa’s work through October 24. San Francisco-born Villa was a groundbreaking, 20th century modern artist whose work explores the meaning of cultural diversity in America. The exhibition, entitled Carlos Villa: Worlds in Collision, focuses mainly on the artist’s drawings, mixed-media painting, and constructions from the 1970s up until his death in 2013. Villa experimented with techniques of Western painting with materials found in non-Western art; the juxtaposition is most notably in the 1970s. The exhibition is a joint effort by the Asian Art Museum and San Francisco Art Institute (SFAI). Visit https://exhibitions. asianart.org/exhibitions/carlos-villa-worlds-in-collision/ to learn more.

articles.text: Johnny Depp reprises his role as Captain Jack Sparrow in Pirates Of The Caribbean: On Stranger Tides. Review by Chris Honoré Pirates Of The Caribbean: On Stranger Tides is Johnny Depp returning once again to his signature role as the charming, strangely androgynous and ever resourceful Captain Jack Sparrow. His costume, his line delivery, his sashaying walk, his raccoon-like eyes are pure, campy genius. And his performance is close to the sole reason to see this fourth installment of what has been a wildly successful franchise. Audiences, of course, are ever hopeful that they will be present for the reincarnation of something as captivating as the Curse of the Black Pearl. Alas, of the films that followed the 2003 Pirates debut, a solid story has been elusive. All of the sequels, regardless of their subtitles, have been either decidedly convoluted or so thin in plot that it’s tempting to just forget the story and simply enjoy the characters. In this latest film the plot has been simplified: find the fountain of youth for England before the Spaniards find it and do something rash. Rumor is, there’s a map. That’s it. The meaning of the subtitle, “On Stranger Tides,” is a mystery. In fact, there are few strangers on any tides in this film. Okay, there is Blackbeard (Ian McShane), who is a nasty piece of work. Also new is the alluring, if duplicitous, Angelica (Penelope Cruz), with whom we’re told Jack has history. Seems that a broken heart was involved. Captain Hector Barbossa (Geoffrey Rush), Jack’s nemesis, returns. As does sidekick, Joshamee Gibbs. They’re all great characters, wonderfully portrayed, and the photography is stunning. But, like its antecedents, with the exception of the original Black Pearl, the current journey of Captain Jack Sparrow seems pedestrian – with the exception of the first 15 minutes that involve an escape by Sparrow and stalwart Joshamee Gibbs. But then, swashbuckling adventure films must have an opening with a huge Wow factor – it’s de rigueur. Often, that first action setup can be the best part of the franchise ride. The reality is that any sequel that follows the first Pirates film is a tough climb. The initial introduction of Captain Jack Sparrow and company was fresh and original, with a winning story, despite the film being named after a Disneyland attraction. The burden of replicating that initial excitement is no easy trick. As demonstrated by On Stranger Tides. Pirates of the Caribbean: On Stranger Tides. Starring Johnny Depp, Penelope Cruz, Ian McShane, Geoffrey Rush, Kevin McNally and Keith Richards. Directed by Rob Marshall. 2 hrs., 16 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2011. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Remarkably, a short story by the science fiction writer Philip K. Dick, adapted for the screen as The Adjustment Bureau, turns out to be the best romance of the year. A different love story to be sure, crafted from an unusual premise. However, because Hollywood has served up an endless string of trivial nonsense, this film comes as a welcome surprise. It begins with Elise Sellas (Emily Blunt), a ballet dancer, and David Norris (Matt Damon), a hotshot politician running for the state senate, meeting cute in the men’s room of the Waldorf Astoria. David is preparing to deliver a very difficult speech. Certain that he’s alone, he begins rehearsing. Suddenly, Elise steps out of one of the stalls. They begin a gentle, smart badinage and their mutual attraction is quickly evident – to them and the audience. But all that has happened to them is part of a greater plan. If either deviates from the plan, a small adjustment will be necessary. Enter stage left, the Adjustment Bureau: men in snap-brim hats, dark suits, and narrow ties, who warn David that he cannot pursue a relationship with Elise, for reasons that are not disclosed. David, impulsive and a bit reckless, is not inclined to cooperate, sensing that in Elise he has met someone unlike anyone before. Perhaps you have to suspend your disbelief to be fully engaged by the story. You must be willing to give the story sufficient latitude, all in the interest of being intrigued and perhaps even surprised. It helps that the fantasy/sci fi aspects of the film are handled so seamlessly that it never seems contrived or in any way jarring. It all fits nicely together. As David grows more intent on pursuing a relationship with Elise, the story delves into the existential question of free will. Do we design our own lives or are there forces greater than ourselves that guides us? Should David be allowed to choose? Are any of us truly free to choose? Of course, in the world of Philip K. Dick the ability to make choices is an illusion. During those periods in history when the Bureau stepped back and let mankind truly choose, the result was the 20th century, one of the most violent in history. Hence, the Bureau concluded that it was time to re-engage and guide. So, David falls down the rabbit hole (where would sci-fi/fantasy be without it?) and sets in motion a test of wills between himself and the Bureau which insists that she cannot be part of his destiny. Acts two and three involve an escalation of tension, some well choreographed chase scenes, as pieces of the puzzle begin to fall into place. If your threshold for such storytelling is high and if your imagination is captured by such a premise, you will find The Adjustment Bureau a solidly entertaining film, a perfect blend of romance and the improbable, nicely imagined and well acted. The Adjustment Bureau. Starring Matt Damon, Emily Blunt, John Slattery, Anthony Mackie and Terrance Stamp. Written and directed by George Nolf. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2011. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: The Adjustment Bureau a fine romance

articles.text: Nº 58 in a series Queen Elizabeth died peacefully at age 96 on Thursday, September 15, at Balmoral Castle in the Scottish countryside. She proved the longest serving monarch in English history, having celebrated her Platinum Jubilee reign of 70 years on June 5. The French government turned to paying tribute to the Grand British Dame. The Eiffel Tower with its typically bright display, a mesmerizing lightshow, went dark into the night. President Emmanuel Macron appeared at the British Embassy in Paris to pay tribute to the queen. He spoke in English to address the British public: “We are grateful for Elizabeth’s deep affection. She is a longtime friend and the closest of allies. Queen Elizabeth mastered our language, loved French culture, and touched our hearts,” he said. He remarked that she visited France more than any other nation. He signed the book of condolences, and First Lady Brigette Macron shared her “very, very great emotion and respect” for the late sovereign. “She was very important to us. For me, she was, she is, and she will remain the queen.” The world responded with condolences to her British subjects. The Italians laid flowers outside Queen Elizabeth and Prince Philip. Queen Elizabeth in graceful majesty. Duke of Windsor Edward and wife Wallis at home in Paris in the early 1960s. the British Embassy in Rome. Pope Francis sent “heartfelt condolences.” At the White House in Washington D.C., the flag was lowered to half-mast. German Chancellor Olaf Scholz paid tribute to the Queen’s wonderful humor and her role for reconciliation after the Second World War. The Bundestag observed a moment of silence. The German Federation president Frank-Walter Steinmeier said, “Her Majesty was held in the highest esteem throughout the world.” Brussels lowered its flags to half-mast, and President of the Council of Europe, Charles Michel, commented about Elizabeth II’s statesmanship, and her monumental presence through the great conflicts of our time. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said the Queen had been a reassuring presence through decades of change as the United Nations held a moment of silence in respect to the queen. Despite becoming a queen by accident, Elizabeth’s reign spanned the terms of seven U.S. Presidents. The princess was age 10 in 1936 when her uncle, King Edward VIII, abdicated the throne, setting in motion her carefully crafted life. Her father became king, crowned George VI, and her heart broke for him in his private struggle to overcome a lifetime of stuttering. (Colin Firth played him in The King’s Speech). Elizabeth dealt with a gripping fear of queen presumptive, while her carefree younger sister Margaret was flippant. Elizabeth was the insular, shy first-born, while Margaret was bold, confident, and boiling-over with envy. The teenage Princess Elizabeth gave a first-time public address over radio airwaves, a patriotic message to her war-torn nation, and her uncle, always quick to lacerate to make a deep wound, chortled over his niece’s high-pitched and childish voice, and pet-named her Shirley Temple. Her uncle Edward’s abandonment of the royal throne was unimaginable to the child princess. She couldn’t fathom his fixation on the American socialite Wallis Simpson, and his reckless scrambling of the succession risking public wrath and ridicule and thrusting her much-loved, unprepared father onto the throne. Why wouldn’t Edward simply behave? Her grandparents, King George V and his Queen Mary, had refused to receive Wallis Simpson after a single meeting. Decades later, the issue of divorce and remarriage reared again. McCutchen Construction In kitchen remodeling, there are many selections to consider for not only a well-designed, functional space but also one that is timeless and beautiful. Among one of the most important steps in remodeling is your choice of countertops. With so many possibilities, the process of selecting the right material can be overwhelming. While there are many options today for a great looking countertop not all will suit your family’s needs. Some popular materials today are Quartzite, Quartz, Marble and Granite. To help you decide the right material for you and your family, let’s explore these options for their strengths as well as their challenges. Quartzite is a natural stone. It’s highly durable and is available in many options aesthetically. This natural stone does require sealing to help protect it from heavy use and to ensure its longevity. It’s best to have it sealed once or twice a year to keep it performing and looking its best. The earth tones of this granite help create a refined, contemporary kitchen design. Classic marble is the star of this vintage style kitchen. Quartz is popular these days and rightfully so. It’s highly durable, scratch and stain resistant, made to last. This is an engineered stone that’s made from small stone particles or powder and combined with resin. Because it’s manmade, it does have less variation in appearance than natural material. Even so, it’s often difficult to tell the difference between this and natural stone once installed, and the cost is much less. Marble is classic, well-loved for its timeless beauty and elegance. However, marble may not be for everyone and certainly not suitable for every space. This is because it’s a relatively porous and soft stone that is easily stained and scratched. It requires sealing more often than most stones. If your kitchen is a high-traffic space, this may not be the best option for you. If you absolutely love it, try to infuse it on an accent wall or a backsplash. Granite has been a top choice for homeowners for many years. It can be found in a range of unique colors and patterns so there are many options to choose from. It is durable, scratch and stain resistant and can withstand high temperatures. This is a porous material and while tough, it does require regular sealing. The price for granite can vary greatly depending on the uniqueness of the slab, the size and the thickness. articles.text: Once again, it’s the season for football games and backto-school activities. And if you work for a medium-size or large employer, it will soon be open enrollment season – the time of year when you can review your employee benefits and make changes as needed. What areas should you focus on? Actually it’s a good idea to pay close attention to all your benefits. Some of the offerings may have changed from last year – and you might have experienced changes in your own life, too, which might lead you to look for something different from your existing benefits package. Health insurance You may want to start with your health insurance. If you’re satisfied with your coverage, and it’s essentially the same as it’s been, you may well want to stick with what you have. However, many employers are increasingly offering high-deductible health plans, which, as the name suggests, could entail more out-ofpocket costs for you. But high-deductible plans may also offer something of benefit: the ability to contribute to a health savings account (HSA). Your HSA contributions are made with pre-tax dollars, so they can reduce your taxable income for the year. Also, your earnings grow tax-free, and your withdrawals are taxfree, provided the money is used for qualified medical expenses. (Withdrawals taken before age 65 that aren’t used for qualified medical expenses are taxable and subject to a 20% penalty; once you reach 65, the penalty no longer applies, although withdrawals are still taxable as income if not used for a qualified expense.) Life insurance Your next benefit to consider: Life insurance. Your employer may offer a group life insurance plan, but you’ll want to evaluate whether it’s sufficient for your needs, especially if you’ve experienced changes in your personal situation over the past year, such as getting married or adding a new child. There’s no magic formula for how much life insurance you need – you’ll need to consider a variety of factors, such as your income, family size, mortgage and so on – but it may be necessary to supplement your employer’s coverage with a private policy. Disability insurance Your employer may also offer disability insurance as a benefit. Some employers’ disability policies are fairly limited, covering only short periods of time, so you may want to consider a private policy. Retirement plan Beyond the various insurance policies your employer may offer, you’ll also want to closely look at your 401(k) or similar retirement plan. Typically, you can make changes to your 401(k) throughout the year, but it’s important to make sure your investment selections and contribution amounts are still aligned with your risk tolerance and goals. Also, are you contributing enough to earn your employer’s match, if one is offered? And if you’ve already receiving the match, can you still afford to put in more to your plan if such a move makes sense for you? Your employee benefits package can be a valuable part of your overall financial strategy. So, as open enrollment season proceeds, take a close look at what you already have, what’s being offered, and what changes you need to make. It will be time well spent. articles.text: Campers gather at the electric wood carving station. Scores of campers, parents and counselors gathered at Hampton Field on a warm Sunday afternoon, September 11, for Camp Augusta’s Campathon, a fundraiser for the non-profit camp established in 1931. The event, which aimed to raise $150,000 to change its ropes course to a pole course, featured more than a dozen stations, which included electric wood carving, acoustic guitar instructions and sword fighting. There were also a photo booth, bracelet making and balloon animals stations. Additionally, the event had more camp-specific games like gaga ball and the Augusta Knowledge Bowl, which asked campers questions about camp history and facilities. Correct questions equaled a punch card mark and ten punch card marks equal a level bracelet. Campers continued leveling up into the early evening. Arguably, the most important feature was Lazy Dog Ice Cream and its giant drumsticks. Based near the camp in Nevada City, Lazy Dog has become a staple for campers and counselors for years. They have unique flavors like strawberry shortcake and sour patch kids. Campers and parents played games one-handed while working through their oversized drumsticks. Lazy Dog even makes specialty cones exclusively for the camp. This was the first in-person fundraising event Camp Augusta has held since the COVID-19-related lockdowns “It felt incredible to be back in person,” said Board President Jason Ring, who touched on the family tradition at the camp and on display at the event. “We have friends in the community whose kids all went to the camp.” Randy Grayson, the Camp Augusta Director, echoed this sentiment and spoke to the Post about the benefit of the transition, the incredibly diverse staff and the unique activities that differentiate Augusta from other summer camps. Grayson also expressed deep gratitude to be returning to in-person events and the unique activities that campers experience at Camp Augusta. “We want to do all things that don’t exist anywhere else in the world. So, with every one of the 25 elements [on display at the Campathon], we want them to be unique, and we want them to have multi-functions. You could do it as a team, you could do it individually, you could do it in a small group, with all sorts of different layered challenges,” Grayson explained. He confirmed that Augusta has long broken away from the cookie-cutter approach to summer camp. “With the constellation of trees [surrounding the camp], we didn’t have all the elements interact with each other in varied ways,” he said. He explained how Augusta’s unique approach to activities and international coalition of counselors keep kids and families coming back year after year. “We do the one event, because the staff are from all over the world. Right now we have [counselors from] six different countries here,” Grayson said. Grayson, whose personal favorite activity is probably the faux sword fighting, will oversee the budgetary responsibilities and big picture considerations of the installation of a new zip line and ropes course using 80-foot poles instead of trees. According to Grayson, the camp has lost nearly 80 percent of its tallest trees in the last 20 years. Ronnie, who Photo by Ian Firstenberg The sword fighting station is ready for campers. Two campers square off for a sword fight while a counselor referees. Counselors teach a camper some riffs in the acoustic guitar booth. hails from Scotland, is the Ropes Course director and will be in charge of logistics, design management and production responsibilities. Sustainability is chief among the benefits of the innovative renovation. The project is slated to cost between $150,000 and $175,000. Construction will be handled by Challenge Works and should begin in early 2023. “On a long-term basis, sustainability is the key because the poles won’t die,” Grayson said. Overall, the Sunday fundraiser in Piedmont was a tremendous success. Kids and parents, full of ice cream, left with smiles knowing that Camp Augusta will continue to provide unique and innovative opportunities for campers, families and counselors. “A big focus of Augusta is creative expression and creative experience. We do the clinic activities like archery, but a large focus is how we make sure kids have a creative experience that they don’t have in their normal lives,” Grayson said. JENNIFER LONG, Incumbent 1) Housing Housing development in Piedmont requires careful, thorough planning that will enhance our safe, beautiful neighborhoods, and ensure continued strong property values. It is also essential to have as many community members as possible weighing in on how best to create housing in our city. Further, Piedmont residents must understand what California law requires of the city (and what it does not) and how we can make our compliance with state law work for our community. Currently, Piedmont has no specific plans to build housing and is under no obligation to pay for housing development. However, the City is mandated by state law to create a plan which identifies potential sites upon which housing might be built. The City is currently working diligently on this necessary step, which ensures that Piedmont will be able to maintain local control over the future of our beloved city. 2) Infrastructure I recently voted with my fellow council members to begin the design process for the renovation of Piedmont’s police and fire dispatch center. This dispatch center is a critical part of our city’s excellent police and fire services. Public safety will continue to be my top priority.
